name: Response contains an actual isAvailable invocation vs. omits the availability check entirely
side_a: No deduct: the constructor body contains at least one invocation of the availability method with a String argument (e.g., `isAvailable(requestedName)` or `isAvailable(nameToCheck)`), regardless of whether the surrounding loop/assignment logic is correct or even terminates.
side_b: Deduct: the response never calls isAvailable (or any availability method) anywhere — it just assigns the name directly — so there is nothing to award the 'calls isAvailable on Account/this with a String' point for.

name: Some availability check + alternate-name logic exists vs. unconditional assignment of requestedName
side_a: No deduct if the code calls isAvailable at least once and, on failure, produces a different candidate name (whether inside a loop or a single if) — the required check/update behavior is present.
side_b: Deduct if the constructor never calls isAvailable and never forms an alternate candidate name, simply assigning the requested name to the field; there is no check-and-update behavior at all to credit.

name: Single conditional retry counts as the required repetition vs. only an explicit loop counts
side_a: No deduct if the student recomputes a candidate name and checks availability even once via an if-statement rather than a loop; a one-shot conditional retry still demonstrates the check-then-update structure.
side_b: Deduct only when there is no control structure at all guarding the assignment — i.e., the name is assigned with no conditional or loop based on availability.

name: An actual counter-advancing statement inside the loop vs merely declaring/using a counter with no increment
side_a: Give the point (no_deduct) only when the code contains a statement that actually advances the counter on each repetition (e.g. `i++`, `count = count + 1`) located inside the repeating construct, so successive attempts use different suffixes.
side_b: Deduct when no statement anywhere advances the counter — a declared-but-frozen counter (`int suffix = 1;` with nothing incrementing it, giving an infinite loop on the same name) or a counter used only once with no increment does not satisfy 'increment count in the context of a loop'.

name: Code attempts names repeatedly vs makes one fixed fallback attempt (or none)
side_a: Give the point (no_deduct) when the code sets up a repeated-attempt structure in which the counter value changes from attempt to attempt.
side_b: Deduct when the code performs at most one fallback attempt (hard-coded `requestedName + 1`) or never builds an alternate name at all, since there is no 'context of a loop' for any increment to live in.

name: An explicit numeric counter variable is declared/initialized vs. no counter at all (suffix omitted or hard-coded literal)
side_a: Credit when the response actually declares and initializes a numeric counter variable that feeds the appended suffix (e.g. `int suffix = 1;` / `int i = 1;`), even if the surrounding loop logic is flawed (missing increment, infinite loop) — the 'initialize the count' requirement is satisfied by the declaration itself.
side_b: Deduct when there is no counter variable to initialize: either the response appends no numeric suffix at all, or it splices a hard-coded literal (`requestedName + 1`) with no counter being declared/initialized/advanced. Absence of a count is treated as failing 'initialize the count', not as a vacuous pass.
